analysis.one_liner: Bans mid-decade congressional redistricting and partisan gerrymandering, with public input and court backup.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: it was referred to the Judiciary Committee on February 7, 2024 and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set rules every state must follow when drawing congressional district lines. It bans redrawing maps between census years just to gain seats, bans maps drawn to favor one party, requires districts to respect the Voting Rights Act and real communities, and requires public hearings, posted maps and data, and comment periods. If a state misses its deadline, a federal three-judge court would draw the map instead.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters of both parties in states where one party draws itself safe seats. The bill targets maps that make general elections uncompetitive by packing or splitting voters, and it requires voting-rights protections for racial and language minorities plus open public processes for drawing and reviewing maps.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a state from using any congressional map drawn with the intent, or having the effect, of materially favoring or disfavoring a political party, measured with standard quantitative fairness tests against the state's recent elections.
Bans mid-decade redistricting: once a state redistricts after an apportionment, it cannot redraw again until after the next census, except when a court requires it.

Requires districts to comply with the Constitution and the Voting Rights Act and to preserve the practical ability of protected groups to elect representatives of their choice, and to keep communities of interest and neighborhoods together where practicable.

Requires the map-drawing entity to hold hearings before and after releasing plans, post all proposed maps, underlying data, and public comments online, provide drawing software the public can use, and release a written evaluation of each plan against external metrics at least 48 hours before any vote.
Bars drawing maps around the homes of incumbent members of Congress and bars using incumbents' party affiliation or voting history as a factor.

If a state misses its deadline, any citizen may sue and a three-judge federal court takes over and draws the map, with public hearings and a chance for comment; the bill also gives the Attorney General and state residents a private right of action to enforce the criteria, with expedited review by the D.C. Circuit en banc.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and state legislative majorities whose parties currently hold extra seats from gerrymandered maps would risk losing safe districts. States would bear the administrative cost of running a more open, documented process, and redistricting consultants and map-drawing software vendors would lose business as opaque insider map-drawing gives way to published data and metrics.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies immediately to existing maps: any state whose current plan does not comply would have to redraw within 45 days of enactment, meaning the same bill that bans mid-decade redistricting would itself force a round of mid-decade redistricting nationwide.

It takes map-drawing power away from elected state bodies when they miss deadlines and hands it to federal three-judge courts, which substitutes judicially drawn maps for politically accountable ones and raises a fair objection about who should decide district lines.

The partisan-fairness test leans on specific statistical measures and a 7%-of-seats (or one-seat) threshold, and courts applying such quantitative tests could themselves shape partisan outcomes; the bill's presumption of violation and automatic stay of a state's map upon filing suit puts existing maps in legal limbo at election time.

Concentrating appeals exclusively in the D.C. Circuit, sitting en banc, funnels every map dispute through one court, which critics could see as channeling politically charged decisions to a single venue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and widely felt: fewer safe seats drawn by the party in power, protections for minority voters, and a transparent process voters can actually see and participate in. The costs are serious design questions rather than monetary ones: rushed compliance for existing maps, judicial takeover of map-drawing when states balk, and contestable statistical thresholds. A better-crafted bill could have addressed the fairness goal with more lead time and more local control; this bill chose speed and court enforcement instead.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the Redistricting Reform Act of 2024 on February 7, 2024, joined by Senator Laphonza Butler.
It was its only action: the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, where no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed.
Its sole cosponsor was one Democrat, leaving it with two Senate supporters out of 100 and no Republican backing.
The Congress ended January 3, 2025, and the bill received no further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and state legislative majorities in gerrymandered states keep the safe-seat maps the bill would have barred, and the map-drawing consultants who serve them keep their business. Nothing changed for voters because nothing happened.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Redistricting Reform Act of 2024 in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after referral; it received no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had two Democratic sponsors and no Republican cosponsor, and it never reached a vote, so no legislator outside the sponsoring party ever had to take a recorded position on it.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majorities
industries.note: The bill bans maps drawn to materially favor a party and forbids drawing around incumbents' residences, threatening the extra safe seats both parties' mapmakers have created. Their current advantage exists by keeping competitive districts off the table, which runs directly against voters' interest in meaningful elections.

industries.industry: Redistricting consultants and map-drawing software vendors
industries.note: Gerrymandering is a paid trade: parties hire consultants and buy software to engineer maps behind closed doors. The bill would require public posting of all data and maps, public drawing tools, and court scrutiny, shrinking the market for insider map-crafting.
